question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old man was sent from a skilled nursing facility to our acute care clinic late this afternoon because the nursing staff observed a new asymmetric fullness of his left calf that had appeared over the past 18 hours when they first stood him at the bedside for physical therapy. Five days earlier he had been admitted to that facility after a community-acquired influenza A pneumonia that had required four days of inpatient intravenous antibiotics; during the first three days of the nursing-home stay his oxygen requirements and generalized fatigue were such that he remained in bed except for brief trips to the bathroom, eating his meals in the supine position and skipping the initial scheduled ambulation sessions. By yesterday his respiratory status had improved and rehabilitation was initiated, at which point the therapists noted that the left trouser leg seemed tighter than the right. The patient himself reports a dull sensation of heaviness confined to the posterior calf when he lowers the limb but denies sharp or focal pain, burning, numbness, tingling, groin mass, fever, chills, color change, or drainage from the skin. He has never been diagnosed with blood clots in the legs or lungs, has no known thrombophilia, and recalls no similar episodes in the past. Medical history is notable for stage 2 chronic kidney disease, well-controlled hypertension on lisinopril 10 mg daily, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes; he has not undergone any surgical procedure in the last year and wears no splints, casts, or braces. Medications are lisinopril, a multivitamin, and as-needed acetaminophen; he is not taking systemic corticosteroids, hormonal therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antithrombotic drugs. He quit smoking three decades ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of whisky on holidays, and does not use illicit substances. There is no family history of venous thrombo-embolism. He recalls bumping the same calf against the wheelchair footrest two evenings ago and wonders whether he might have strained a muscle while coughing vigorously during the pneumonia, both of which he believes could explain the swelling. On arrival to our unit—before receiving analgesics, intravenous fluids, compression, or anticoagulant therapy—he was sitting in a recliner with the legs dangling. Nursing triage vitals were temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 126/72 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats min⁻¹ and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 96 % on 2 L min⁻¹ nasal cannula, identical to his baseline flow at the facility. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed a normal S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops and clear breath sounds except for faint inspiratory crackles at the left base that have been stable since discharge from the hospital. The abdomen was soft and nontender; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites was appreciated. Inspection of the lower extremities showed that the left calf appeared subtly more convex posteriorly than the right, while the thigh, knee, ankle, and foot contours were symmetric. A cloth tape placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 41.7 cm on the left versus 38.1 cm on the right, documenting a 3.6 cm difference. Fifteen centimeters above the patella both thighs measured 55.0 cm, and around the malleoli the girths were 27.4 cm left and 27.0 cm right. After the leg hung dependent for 30 seconds a lattice of straight, bluish superficial vessels became prominent along the posteromedial calf and collapsed completely when the limb was elevated, distinguishing them from chronic varicosities. The skin was warm but retained a uniform pink color with no erythema, brawny discoloration, or weeping; there was no induration, crepitus, or fluctuance, and thumb indentation over the tibial crest rebounded immediately without leaving a pit. Gentle palpation tracing the expected course of the femoral, popliteal, and posterior tibial veins elicited no discrete point tenderness or palpable cord; squeezing the gastrocnemius reproduced only a dull stretch sensation. Knee and ankle ranges of motion were full and painless, straight-leg raise provoked no discomfort, and distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2 + bilaterally with capillary refill to all toes under two seconds. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was intact, and motor strength in the lower extremities was 5/5 except for mild deconditioning-related fatigue. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was appreciated. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained before blood sampling demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats min⁻¹ without ST-T abnormalities. Point-of-care laboratory analysis drawn prior to any intervention showed hemoglobin 13.2 g dL⁻¹, leukocytes 7.0 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelet count 234 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, serum sodium 138 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 1.32 mg dL⁻¹ (baseline 1.28 mg dL⁻¹), AST 21 U L⁻¹, ALT 18 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph ordered by the facility earlier today showed persistent mild bibasilar infiltrates but no new consolidation or pleural effusion. Given the recent prolonged bed rest followed by sudden asymmetric calf enlargement exceeding three centimetres, yet with the possibility of a post-traumatic muscular hematoma or localized soft-tissue injury from coughing or the wheelchair incident appearing equally credible in the absence of focal deep venous tenderness, the decision was made to obtain a comprehensive duplex ultrasound of the left iliac, femoral, popliteal, and infrapopliteal venous segments while the patient remains hemodynamically stable and prior to any administration of anticoagulation.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score adds 1 point per qualifying risk factor or examination finding and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
- Recently bedridden for at least 3 days or recent major surgery: the first 3 days of the facility stay were spent in bed except for bathroom trips = +1.
- Calf swelling ≥3 cm, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: 41.7 − 38.1 = 3.6 cm = +1.
- Nonvaricose collateral superficial veins on the symptomatic calf = +1.
- No active cancer, prior DVT, leg paralysis/paresis or cast immobilization, deep venous tenderness, entire-leg swelling, or unilateral pitting edema: 0 each.
- Traumatic hematoma or localized soft-tissue injury is judged as likely as DVT = −2.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 − 2 = 1.
Final answer: 1
